column3: It directly presents taking gods besides Allah in expectation of help, exposing the false worship order named by the focus.
Divine willing that immediately realizes its object provides only a broad contrast to human desire being wrongly directed.
It identifies other gods as objects adopted for honor, giving a concrete motive for the false choice questioned in the focus.
Its rhetorical denial of worshipped gods besides the Merciful reinforces the focus's rejection of rival deities.
The immediate Abraham narrative begins the same local diagnosis of sound devotion that frames the focus's question.
Calling a report manifest falsehood offers a limited parallel to the focus's charge of false construction.
It contrasts seeking worldly increase with intending Allah's face, clarifying that desire may be directed toward different ends.
The next local question about their expectation of the Lord sharpens the focus's challenge to their chosen gods.
The affak is characterized as persistently false and sinful, supplying a personal form of the focus's falsehood.
Its question about taking gods besides the Merciful shows their inability to avert harm, directly testing the focus's desired objects.
The realization of divine will does not specifically address the false gods or false desire in the focus.
Being turned away from truth portrays deviation as an active redirection, resonating with the focus's misdirected willing.
It joins gods besides Allah, their failure to help, and fabricated falsehood in one close parallel to the focus.
Abraham's sound heart supplies the positive devotional integrity opposed to the focus's false preference.
The declaration of Allah's oneness establishes the exclusive divine reality against which the focus's plural gods are false.
It explicitly combines worshipping idols besides Allah with fabricating falsehood and redirects provision-seeking to Allah.
Wanting Allah, His messenger, and the Hereafter offers a constructive alternative to directing desire toward false gods.
Its false claims about Allah culminate in the question of how people are turned away, closely echoing the focus's false direction.
The warning that a request can turn from faith to disbelief gives only a general example of desire taking a wrong course.
The immediately preceding question about what they worship directly sets up the focus's accusation of false gods.
Those following desires seek a great deviation for others, clarifying desire as a force that can redirect people from the right way.
The verse's concern with a worldly aim is a remote parallel to wrongly oriented desire.
Spectators' wish for Qarun's wealth shows covetous desire, but not worship or falsehood about Allah.
The objection to making the gods one exposes resistance to the exclusive worship premise underlying the focus.
Doubt about the Creator provides a broad background for rejecting the exclusive divine orientation of the focus.
Abraham's local maneuver belongs to the same confrontation with idol worship that the focus will diagnose.
Naming Allah as the God of humanity supports exclusive allegiance, though it does not address the false choice directly.
The overturned city supplies an image of reversal but adds little to false worship or intentional preference.
Its denial of another god beside Allah reinforces the exclusive deity asserted against the focus's alternatives.
The human dependence of alleged divine figures undermines treating them as gods alongside Allah.
The same surah explicitly calls their statement a lying fabrication, directly illuminating the focus's opening charge of falsehood.
Abraham's local excuse advances the idol narrative but does not itself explain false worship.
Devils descending upon habitual liars gives a concrete setting for the falsehood signaled in the focus.
The reaction to the call for one god makes clear that exclusive worship disrupts an established network of rival gods.
Universal fear of the Lord above gives a general contrast to honoring other gods.
The consecrated she-camel does not materially clarify false gods, falsehood, or directed desire.
It challenges whether earthborn gods can create or revive, weakening the deity status sought in the focus.
Abraham's withdrawal follows the idol confrontation and advances the local contrast between false worship and integrity.
After identifying Allah as Creator, it asks how people are turned away, closely matching the focus's diagnosis of false direction.
Its rhetorical refusal to worship another besides Allah directly opposes the false gods the focus asks about.
The reference to plotting does not add a specific connection to false worship or misdirected desire.
Divine effectiveness in what He wills is only a general contrast to the human wanting questioned in the focus.
The challenge to examine what they worship opens the same critical scrutiny of chosen worship objects.
Pharaoh's conjectural claim about Moses' God shows arrogant distortion of the divine question, though less directly than earlier cards.
Acknowledging Allah as Creator while being turned away exposes the disconnect between recognition and actual allegiance.
Turning one's longing toward the Lord provides a concise positive alternative to desiring gods besides Allah.
The divine intention to establish the oppressed is not a useful link to false worship or false desire.
Guidance of whomever Allah wills gives only a general frame for right direction.
The claimed identity as Allah's devoted servants belongs to the same surah's dispute over genuine versus false devotion.
The intended favor for the oppressed is not materially connected to the focus's worship question.
Moses' staff swallowing what they falsify gives a vivid counteraction to fabricated deception, without addressing gods directly.
It argues that multiple gods besides Allah would corrupt the order of creation, directly contesting the plurality desired in the focus.
The idolaters' command to defend their gods displays committed loyalty to the false objects challenged by the focus.
It questions any force that can aid people besides the Merciful, undermining reliance on alternatives to Allah.
Divine sufficiency against mockers does not specifically clarify the focus's false gods or desire.
The crowd's stated desire supplies a distant example of desire resisting a corrective boundary.
Divine support against possible deception is not a substantive link to false worship.
It explicitly joins taking gods besides Allah with inventing a lie about Him, closely mirroring both poles of the focus.
The failed plot against Abraham belongs to the idol narrative but adds little beyond earlier direct cards.
The denial of Allah's signs is linked to being turned away, extending the focus's diagnosis of redirected judgment.
Treating Allah as behind one's back depicts a displaced allegiance that helps explain choosing other objects instead.
Allah's lack of need from His servants corrects a broad misunderstanding of worship, but not the focus's false gods.
Human desire to continue in wrongdoing offers a general parallel to willing a course known to be wrong.
The prohibition on taking other protectors instead of believers shows a misplaced choice of allegiance, though outside worship proper.
The admission that humans and jinn should not speak lies about Allah directly supports the focus's charge of false attribution.
The sinners' false assessment at the Hour reflects distortion, but not the focus's specific religious choice.
It denies that anyone besides Allah can remove the impending reality, exposing the impotence of alternatives to Him.
Abraham's resolve against idols belongs to the same confrontation but is less informative after the direct idol texts.
Acting for Allah's face while seeking no human return models desire and intention correctly directed to Allah.
The local judgment scene sends those who worshipped besides Allah toward Hell, showing the end of the false path questioned in the focus.
Allah's exclusive provision and strength counter the imagined powers that make rival gods desirable.
Its account of desire choosing a prohibited alternative is a formal but distant parallel to misdirected wanting.
It asks whether gods besides Allah can help or help themselves, directly exposing the uselessness of the focus's desired deities.
Human willing's dependence on Allah's will is only a broad theological contrast to the focus's human desire.
Those who name Allah as Creator are nevertheless described as turned away, closely exposing the contradiction behind false allegiance.
It directly questions worshipping besides Allah what controls neither harm nor benefit, testing the legitimacy of the focus's gods.
Uncertainty over intended harm or guidance does not meaningfully illuminate false gods or falsehood.
It denies any protector or helper besides Allah, reinforcing the exclusivity that makes rival reliance false.
It rejects testifying that other gods exist with Allah and declares freedom from association, directly answering the focus's plurality.
The option to remember gives a limited formal link to willing, without the false worship context.
Calling revelation an invented falsehood illustrates the same kind of false attribution, though directed against the Quran.
It denies any creator or god but Allah and asks how people are turned away, combining exclusive deity with the focus's diversion theme.
The crowd's harmful desire is a remote analogy for desire overriding a right boundary.
The proposed marriage and labor terms do not contribute to the focus's religious diagnosis.
It denies any protector or helper besides Allah, supporting the exclusivity violated by seeking alternatives.
The command not to obey a sinner or disbeliever gives a general behavioral contrast, not a direct worship link.
The disputed attribution of violent intent is too distant from false worship and worship-directed desire.
It contrasts acknowledging Allah as Creator with invoking powerless beings besides Him against harm or mercy, directly clarifying the false choice.
The descent of the Quran does not add a specific connection to the focus's false gods.
It explicitly rejects taking Jesus and his mother as two gods besides Allah, a direct counterpart to the focus's question.
The generic command to fear Allah and obey the messenger does not add to the already established false-worship diagnosis.
The same surah calls the claim that Allah fathered a child a lie, extending its polemic against false statements about Him.
Faith in guidance is joined to the refusal to associate anyone with the Lord, giving a clear positive alternative.
The command to fear Allah in a social conflict does not materially clarify false gods or false desire.
The account of forbidden private counsel is unrelated to the focus's worship and falsehood theme.
Hearts absorbed elsewhere and works other than the right course offer only a broad image of misplaced orientation.
Self-sufficiency alone does not establish a useful connection to false gods or intentional false worship.
The saved speaker's near ruin by a companion gives a loose local image of being drawn toward destruction.
The practice of zakah does not specifically clarify the focus's charge against false worship.
It contrasts intending the harvest of the Hereafter with intending worldly gain, showing desire's destination shapes its outcome.
It describes people taking rivals besides Allah and loving them as they should love Allah, directly exposing diverted devotion.
It rejects deifying the Messiah and affirms Allah alone as the one to worship, directly countering false godhood.
Abraham's question about taking idols as gods directly parallels the focus's challenge to desiring gods besides Allah.
It condemns assigning partners and fabricated offspring claims to Allah, joining association with false attribution.
It challenges idols that cannot create and are themselves created, undermining their status as desired gods.
Taking religious authorities as lords besides Allah gives a concrete form of displaced worship and allegiance.
It describes worshipping besides Allah what neither harms nor benefits and falsely claiming intercession from it.
The judgment scene separates alleged partners from their worshippers and denies that those partners received the worship.
It calls the many worshiped names unauthorized and commands worship of Allah alone, directly answering the focus's plurality.
It challenges assigning partners to Allah who create like Him, exposing the incoherence of rival divine claims.
Abraham asks that he and his descendants be kept away from worshipping idols, giving a direct opposite desire.
It states that beings called besides Allah create nothing and are themselves created, contesting their divine status.
The universal command to worship Allah and avoid false powers provides the positive alternative to the focus's choice.
It condemns worshipping besides Allah what has no power to provide, directly stripping rival gods of their claimed function.
It forbids setting another god alongside Allah and names the resulting blame and abandonment.
It challenges those invoked besides Allah as unable to remove or redirect affliction, directly testing false reliance.
It shows that those invoked themselves seek nearness to Allah, reversing the hierarchy assumed in false worship.
The calf is presented as a falsely proposed god, a close narrative instance of calling an invented object divine.
It declares Allah alone the God and excludes every other deity, directly opposing the focus's plural gods.
It asks whether gods besides Allah have been taken without proof, closely matching the focus's interrogative exposure.
The repeated prophetic message that there is no god but Allah gives the explicit alternative to all rival worship.
It describes calling on besides Allah what can neither harm nor benefit and calls this far error.
It contrasts Allah as the Truth with what is called on besides Him as falsehood, directly echoing the focus's opening charge.
It condemns calling on another god with Allah without proof and places the claim under divine judgment.
It rejects gods taken besides Allah that create nothing and lack control over harm, benefit, death, or life.
Taking one's own desire as a god directly connects the focus's language of desiring gods with desire itself becoming an object of worship.
It forbids calling on another god with Allah, reinforcing the exclusive allegiance at stake.
Abraham's opening question about what his people worship prepares the same exposure of inherited idol devotion.
It prohibits invoking another god with Allah, directly preserving exclusive worship.
Its repeated question whether any god is with Allah directly contests the plurality presumed by the focus.
The summons of alleged partners at judgment exposes the absence of the gods people claimed.
It forbids calling on another god with Allah and declares that every claimed deity besides Him perishes.
It identifies idols as a worldly bond that will become mutual denial at judgment, showing the collapse of false allegiance.
It challenges those called besides Allah as possessing no share or power in the heavens or earth.
Abraham asks whether they worship what their own hands carve, directly exposing the constructed character of their gods.
It declares pure religion to be Allah's and rejects protectors taken besides Him as supposed mediators.
It describes aversion when Allah alone is mentioned and pleasure when others are mentioned, illuminating a desire for rivals.
It identifies the error of rejecting belief when Allah alone is called upon but believing when partners are associated with Him.
It forbids worshipping those called besides Allah and directs worship to the Lord of all worlds.
It forbids worshipping the sun and moon and commands worship of Allah who created them.
Taking desire as a god is a direct conceptual counterpart to the focus's interrogation of what people desire as gods.
It calls the one who invokes besides Allah what cannot answer until the Day of Resurrection the most astray.
It prohibits setting another god with Allah and frames exclusive return to Him as the warning's direction.
The named female deities introduce a concrete catalogue of the rival gods whose claims the following verses dismantle.
It calls the rival gods mere names unsupported by authority and follows human conjecture and desire, closely joining falsehood and willing.
The listed ancestral idols show how false gods can be preserved as a collective inherited commitment.
It commands that no one be invoked alongside Allah, directly negating the focus's gods besides Him.
